variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: Rate limiting is an admission policy that bounds how much work an identity may ask a resource to perform. For each operation, a limiter identifies the caller, selects the applicable policy, observes prior usage, and returns a decision: admit now, reject, delay, or queue.
variants.prompt: Match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Name the caller
pairs.detail: Use a trusted user, API key, tenant, workload, or network signal.
pairs.explanation: Use a trusted user, API key, tenant, workload, or network signal. An IP address can represent many users behind NAT and one user can rotate addresses.

pairs.label: Scope the work
pairs.detail: Protect an endpoint, operation class, tenant partition, downstream dependency, or service-wide budget.
pairs.explanation: Protect an endpoint, operation class, tenant partition, downstream dependency, or service-wide budget. Expensive writes may need a different policy from cheap reads.

pairs.label: Charge a cost
pairs.detail: One request can cost one unit, while batch size, tokens, rows, bytes, or compute time can consume weighted units when request counts hide the real load.
pairs.explanation: One request can cost one unit, while batch size, tokens, rows, bytes, or compute time can consume weighted units when request counts hide the real load.

pairs.label: Define overflow
pairs.detail: Reject immediately when waiting is unsafe, or use a bounded queue when delayed work is part of the product contract.
pairs.explanation: Reject immediately when waiting is unsafe, or use a bounded queue when delayed work is part of the product contract. Never create an unbounded hidden backlog.

variants.hint:
Name the caller: Use a trusted user, API key, tenant, workload, or network signal.

Scope the work: Protect an endpoint, operation class, tenant partition, downstream dependency, or service-wide budget.

Charge a cost: One request can cost one unit, while batch size, tokens, rows, bytes, or compute time can consume weighted units when request counts hide the real load.

Define overflow: Reject immediately when waiting is unsafe, or use a bounded queue when delayed work is part of the product contract.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Keeping these boundaries clear helps you find the place to change when the system behaves unexpectedly.

variants.prompt: Match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Token bucket
pairs.detail: Refill credit at rate r up to capacity b.
pairs.explanation: Refill credit at rate r up to capacity b. Use it when controlled bursts are valid but the long-term admitted rate must remain bounded. Weighted operations consume more than one token.

pairs.label: Leaky-bucket shaper
pairs.detail: Place work in a bounded queue and release it at a configured rate.
pairs.explanation: Place work in a bounded queue and release it at a configured rate. RFC 3290 distinguishes this shaping behavior from a token-bucket meter. Queue length and maximum waiting time must be explicit.

pairs.label: Fixed-window counter
pairs.detail: Count operations in named intervals and reset at the boundary.
pairs.explanation: Count operations in named intervals and reset at the boundary. It is easy to reason about, but one allowance just before reset and another just after can create a concentrated boundary burst.

pairs.label: Sliding window
pairs.detail: Keep exact timestamps or estimate the moving interval from bounded counters.
pairs.explanation: Keep exact timestamps or estimate the moving interval from bounded counters. Exact logs make membership visible but grow with admitted activity; estimates trade precision for bounded state.

Leaky-bucket shaper: Place work in a bounded queue and release it at a configured rate.

Fixed-window counter: Count operations in named intervals and reset at the boundary.

Sliding window: Keep exact timestamps or estimate the moving interval from bounded counters.

pairs.label: Derive a trusted key
pairs.detail: Combine the authenticated identity, protected resource, policy version, and any intentional tenant boundary.
pairs.explanation: Combine the authenticated identity, protected resource, policy version, and any intentional tenant boundary. Normalize proxy and network signals before using them.

pairs.label: Evaluate atomically
pairs.detail: Refill or expire prior usage, compare the operation cost with available credit, and record the decision as one atomic state transition.
pairs.explanation: Refill or expire prior usage, compare the operation cost with available credit, and record the decision as one atomic state transition.

pairs.label: Apply overflow behavior
pairs.detail: Admit the request, reject it, or enter a bounded queue.
pairs.explanation: Admit the request, reject it, or enter a bounded queue. Keep the limiter timeout smaller than the protected operation's budget.

pairs.label: Return a usable contract
pairs.detail: Explain the policy scope and recovery behavior without exposing sensitive identity or internal topology details.
pairs.explanation: Explain the policy scope and recovery behavior without exposing sensitive identity or internal topology details.

variants.prompt: A token bucket starts full with capacity 30 and refills 10 tokens per second. What does capacity control most directly?
options: The sustained average admitted rate
The amount of short-term burst credit that can be stored
The network latency of the counter store
The number of limiter replicas
variants.explanation: Bucket capacity bounds stored credit and therefore the opening burst. The refill rate controls how quickly credit returns and the long-term sustainable rate.

variants.prompt: Why can a fixed-window counter admit close to two window limits over a short boundary-spanning interval?
options: Requests near the end of one window and the start of the next use different counters
Fixed windows never reset their counters
Every request consumes two units
HTTP automatically retries every rejected request

variants.prompt: A 429 response includes `Retry-After: 12`. What is the safest immediate client behavior?
options: Retry continuously until one request succeeds
Wait at least the advertised delay before the follow-up request
Treat 12 as the remaining request count
Send the same request from many IP addresses
variants.explanation: Retry-After delay-seconds tells the user agent how long it ought to wait. Retrying earlier adds rejected work and can intensify pressure on the protected path.

variants.prompt: Why should a distributed limiter update its decision state atomically?
options: To make every request use the same IP address
To prevent concurrent checks from spending the same remaining quota
To guarantee that all regions are always reachable
To eliminate the need for an identity key
variants.explanation: A separate read, decision, and write can race. Atomic evaluation ensures concurrent requests cannot all observe the same available token or counter value and then admit themselves.
